title: CDN
subtitle: Anycast edge termination, origin shielding, cache invalidation, and absorbing traffic spikes.
keyTakeaways: CDNs terminate TLS and TCP handshakes at hundreds of edge Points of Presence (POPs) near users, cutting round-trip latency and absorbing 90%+ of read traffic.
Origin Shielding places a centralized caching tier between edge POPs and the backend origin, coalescing simultaneous misses into a single origin request to prevent thundering herds.
Use content-addressed immutable URLs for static assets and combine stale-while-revalidate with Surrogate Keys for dynamic APIs to allow immediate invalidation without latency spikes.

sections.heading: Edge Termination and Origin Shielding Mechanics
sections.body: CDNs do much more than store static JPEG files. By advertising identical IP addresses from hundreds of locations worldwide using BGP Anycast, a CDN terminates client TCP and TLS handshakes locally, eliminating multiple round trips across long-haul undersea fiber.
bullets: Anycast edge routing: A user in London connects to an edge server in London, completing the TLS handshake in under 15ms instead of waiting 85ms for a round trip to a US-East origin. Once connected, requests travel over optimized, persistent private backbone networks.

Origin Shielding: When 300 global edge POPs experience cache misses simultaneously, sending all 300 requests directly to the origin can trigger a thundering-herd crash. An Origin Shield acts as a regional caching parent, coalescing identical requests into a single backend fetch.
Connection reuse: Edge POPs maintain persistent, pre-warmed connection pools to the origin, removing the overhead of per-request TCP handshakes and TLS renegotiation.

codeSnippet.title: Production Cache-Control & Surrogate-Key Headers for Edge Resilience

sections.heading: Cache Key Design, Invalidation, and Serving Stale on Origin Failure
sections.body: A CDN's effectiveness depends heavily on its Cache Hit Ratio (CHR). Poor cache key discipline can fragment the cache, causing hit rates to plummet from 95% down to 20%.
bullets: Normalizing cache keys: Strip unnecessary query parameters (like marketing tags `utm_source` or `fbclid`) and sort remaining query params alphabetically (`?a=1&b=2` instead of `?b=2&a=1`) so identical requests map to the same cached object.

Surrogate Keys and tag-based purging: Tag cached objects with metadata headers (`Surrogate-Key: product_4921 category_18`). When an item updates, emit a single API call to purge all objects associated with that tag globally within 150ms.

Serving stale during origin failures: Using `stale-if-error=86400` in the `Cache-Control` header instructs CDN edge nodes to serve expired cached content if the origin returns HTTP 5xx or fails health checks, keeping the site functional during backend outages.

tradeOffs.pros: Absorbs 95%+ of traffic at the edge; sub-20ms response times for users worldwide; protects origin from spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Risk of serving stale data if invalidation webhooks fail or drop; requires strict cache-key normalization discipline.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Product catalogs, media streaming manifests, news articles, and static web assets.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees strictly fresh data on every request with zero risk of cache inconsistency.
tradeOffs.cons: Every request hits the origin backend; higher cloud egress costs and longer latency for geographically distant users.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Personalized bank account balances, checkout payment authorization, and real-time trading order books.

interviewTip: When asked how to protect an origin backend during high-traffic events, highlight Origin Shielding with request collapsing (coalescing). Explain how this ensures that hundreds of edge POPs querying the same expired resource result in only one request hitting the origin.
